speaking.text: Bamboo is a grass rather than a tree, and some species grow almost a metre in a single day. The stem emerges at its final diameter and simply extends, which is why a bamboo pole never thickens with age and why a stand can be harvested indefinitely without replanting anything.

The compass reached Europe several centuries after it was described in China, and its first recorded use there was not for navigation at sea. Surveyors used it to align buildings and to establish property boundaries, and only later did anyone trust it enough to steer by out of sight of land.

Photographic film recorded an image chemically, so a photographer could not know whether a picture had worked until the roll was developed. This delay shaped the practice of the medium: exposures were rationed, compositions were considered at length, and the habit of taking a dozen frames of the same subject arrived only with the digital sensor.

Enzymes accelerate reactions that would otherwise take years, and they do so without being consumed. Each one holds two molecules in precisely the orientation required for them to react, which removes most of the difficulty from a process that would otherwise depend on a chance collision at exactly the right angle.

The Bayeux Tapestry is not a tapestry but an embroidery, and it was almost certainly made in England rather than in France. It survives partly through luck: during the French Revolution it was requisitioned as a wagon cover and rescued by a lawyer who recognised what was about to be cut up.

Fog forms when air cools to the point at which it can no longer hold its moisture, but it disperses for reasons that have little to do with warmth. Wind mixes the saturated layer with drier air above it, which is why a still, cold morning can remain thick with fog long after the sun has risen.

chart.title: Proposed pedestrianisation of the market quarter

lecture.transcript: I want to look at how we know what the inside of the earth is made of, because nobody has ever been anywhere near it. The deepest borehole ever drilled reached about twelve kilometres, which sounds impressive until you realise the radius of the planet is over six thousand. So the interior is inferred entirely, and it is inferred principally from earthquakes. When a large earthquake occurs, it sends out two kinds of wave. Pressure waves compress the material in front of them and can travel through anything. Shear waves move material sideways and cannot pass through a liquid at all, because a liquid offers no resistance to being sheared. Now, seismometers all over the world record both kinds after a distant earthquake, and in the nineteen thirties it became clear that there is a region on the far side of the planet where the pressure waves arrive but the shear waves never do. That shadow zone is the evidence for a liquid outer core, and its size and shape give you the depth at which the liquid begins. Later work found that pressure waves entering the very centre speed up again, which indicates that the innermost core is solid despite being hotter, because the pressure there is high enough to force it back into a solid state. What I want you to take away is the structure of the argument. We have no sample and no possibility of one. What we have is a wave that behaves differently in different materials, and a planet full of instruments listening to it.
key: the deepest borehole reaches twelve kilometres against a radius of over six thousand, so the interior is inferred
earthquakes produce pressure waves that pass through anything and shear waves that cannot cross a liquid
a shadow zone where pressure waves arrive but shear waves do not indicates a liquid outer core
the shape of the shadow zone gives the depth at which the liquid begins
pressure waves speeding up at the centre indicate a solid inner core held solid by pressure despite the heat
the whole picture comes from waves behaving differently in different materials, with no sample available

lecture.transcript: Today I want to discuss why translation of poetry is generally considered impossible, and why people nevertheless keep doing it. The difficulty is not vocabulary. Any competent translator can find an equivalent word. The difficulty is that a poem carries meaning through several channels simultaneously, and these channels are attached to the particular language in ways that cannot be transferred together. Consider what is happening at once. There is the semantic content, what the words denote. There is the sound: rhyme, rhythm, the texture of consonants. There is the register, whether a word feels archaic or colloquial. There is allusion, the way a phrase gestures at earlier literature the original audience would recognise. And there is the shape on the page. A translator can preserve any two or three of these. Preserving all of them is not merely difficult but structurally impossible, because the sound of a word in one language has no relationship to the sound of its equivalent in another. So every translation is a set of decisions about what to sacrifice, and the interesting thing is that the decisions are visible. Compare three English versions of the same Greek poem and you can reconstruct what each translator valued: one has kept the metre and flattened the imagery, another has preserved the images and abandoned the music entirely. This is why some scholars argue that a poem is best represented not by one translation but by several read together, on the grounds that the original sits somewhere in the space between them.

swt.passage: The decision to build a bridge or a tunnel across a strait is usually presented as an engineering judgement, and it is very often a political one. Engineering does narrow the field: a strait carrying heavy shipping may make a bridge with adequate clearance prohibitively tall, and unstable seabed geology can make boring impractical. Within those constraints, however, the choice is frequently determined by considerations that appear nowhere in the technical assessment. A bridge is visible, and visibility is politically valuable to whoever authorised it; a tunnel, once complete, is indistinguishable from the road leading into it. Bridges also generate a photograph, and a project that can be photographed under construction sustains public support through the years when it is producing nothing else. Against this, tunnels are less vulnerable to weather closure, do not obstruct shipping, and have lower long-term maintenance costs in exposed marine environments, which means the cheaper option over sixty years is often the one that is harder to campaign on. Several governments have commissioned comparative studies and then selected the option the study advised against, which is not necessarily irrational: a project that is never authorised has an operating cost of zero and a benefit to match.
key: engineering constraints narrow the choice but rarely determine it

swt.passage: The reintroduction of large predators has become the most visible and most contested branch of conservation, and the arguments on each side are frequently about different questions. Ecologists point to trophic cascades: where wolves were returned to Yellowstone, elk altered their grazing behaviour, browsed vegetation recovered along watercourses, and beaver and songbird populations followed. The mechanism is real, though the Yellowstone case has been oversold, since the same period saw changes in climate, hunting pressure and bear numbers that contributed to the same outcome. Farmers respond to a different question entirely. The cost of a returning predator does not fall on the public that supports the reintroduction; it falls on a small number of people whose livestock are killed, and compensation schemes reliably underpay because they require proof of a cause of death that is frequently impossible to establish. Where reintroduction has succeeded politically, it has generally involved paying for prevention rather than for losses: funding fencing, guardian animals and shepherding before any animal is killed. This is more expensive and considerably less satisfying than compensation, and it works because it addresses the objection people actually have, which is not the money but the experience of finding the animals dead.
key: ecologists cite trophic cascades, as when wolves returned to Yellowstone
the Yellowstone case is overstated because climate, hunting and bear numbers also changed
the costs fall on a few livestock owners while the benefits are diffuse
compensation underpays because proving cause of death is often impossible
successful schemes fund prevention such as fencing and guardian animals rather than paying for losses

essay.prompt: Some people believe that public museums should return artefacts to the countries they were originally taken from, while others argue that major international collections allow more people to see and study them. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write 200-300 words.

reading.passage: Behavioural nudges have been adopted enthusiastically by governments, partly because they are cheap and partly because they avoid the political cost of prohibition. The evidence base is more mixed than the enthusiasm suggests. Default enrolment in pension schemes has produced large and durable effects, and it remains the strongest case anyone can cite. Many other interventions, particularly those relying on informational framing or social comparison messages, show effects that are statistically detectable, practically small, and prone to decay once the novelty passes. A recent analysis comparing published nudge studies with the results of large government trials found effect sizes in the trials roughly one sixth of those in the literature, a gap attributed largely to publication bias rather than to any failure of implementation. None of this argues against using nudges. It argues against treating them as a substitute for regulation in cases where the underlying problem is structural, since a well-designed default cannot address a price that people cannot afford.

reading.passage: Charitable giving is frequently analysed as though donors were purchasing outcomes, and the persistent finding that they respond weakly to information about effectiveness is treated as a puzzle to be corrected. An alternative reading is that donors are not purchasing outcomes at all. They are purchasing participation in something, and the evidence supports this reasonably well: giving rises sharply with personal connection to a cause, with vividness of a single identified beneficiary, and with the visibility of the donation to others, none of which correlates with how much good the money does. Organisations that have tried to compete on measured effectiveness have found the market for that product real but small. This is not an argument for concealing effectiveness data. It is an argument against designing appeals on the assumption that donors will behave as investors when they consistently behave as participants.
reading.q: What does the author suggest about donor behaviour?
options: Donors act as participants in a cause rather than as purchasers of outcomes.
Donors carefully compare charities on measured effectiveness before giving.
Effectiveness data should be withheld because it discourages giving.
Personal connection to a cause has little influence on the amount donated.

reading.passage: The claim that reading on screen produces worse comprehension than reading on paper has been repeated so often that it is treated as settled, and the research is more equivocal than that. The effect appears reliably for expository text read under time pressure, and it largely disappears for narrative text and for readers permitted to work at their own pace. Where it does appear, the most persuasive explanation is not the medium itself but a habit imported into it: people scroll rapidly through screens because most of what they encounter on a screen rewards scrolling rapidly, and they carry that behaviour into material that does not. This matters because the implication is quite different. If the medium were the cause, the remedy would be paper. If the habit is the cause, the remedy is reading differently, which is available on either.
reading.q: What is the author's central point?
options: The comprehension gap probably reflects reading habits carried onto screens rather than the medium itself.
Screen reading has been conclusively shown to impair comprehension of all text types.
Narrative text is comprehended better on screen than on paper.
Time pressure has no measurable effect on reading comprehension.

listening.transcript: I want to talk about the history of handwashing in hospitals, because it is a case where the evidence was overwhelming, the argument was correct, and it failed anyway. In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis was working in a Vienna maternity hospital with two clinics. One was staffed by doctors and medical students, the other by midwives. The death rate from puerperal fever in the doctors' clinic was about three times higher, and this was public knowledge; women begged to be admitted to the midwives' side, and some gave birth in the street rather than enter the wrong door. Semmelweis worked through the possible explanations methodically and eliminated them one by one. The breakthrough came when a colleague cut his finger during an autopsy and died of symptoms identical to the disease killing the mothers. Semmelweis inferred that something was being carried from the dissection room on the hands of doctors, who went straight from autopsies to deliveries, while midwives performed no autopsies at all. He instituted washing in chlorinated lime, and mortality in his clinic fell by roughly ninety per cent within months. Now, why did this not immediately transform medicine? Partly because Semmelweis published almost nothing for fourteen years and then wrote in a tone that insulted everyone he needed to persuade. Partly because he could offer no mechanism; germ theory did not exist yet, and he was effectively asking physicians to accept that an invisible something was being transferred. But mostly, I think, because the claim was unbearable. He was not telling them about a disease. He was telling them that they were the cause of it, and there is no comfortable way to hear that.
key: two Vienna clinics had death rates differing by a factor of three, doctors' worse than midwives'
Semmelweis eliminated alternative explanations methodically
a colleague's death after an autopsy cut suggested transfer from the dissection room
handwashing in chlorinated lime cut mortality by about ninety per cent
the finding was resisted because he published late and antagonised colleagues, and could offer no mechanism before germ theory
most fundamentally, the claim held doctors themselves responsible

listening.transcript: Sand has become one of the most heavily extracted materials on earth, and the shortage is more specific than it first [appears]. I want to say something about why the phrase 'survival of the fittest' causes so much trouble, because the difficulty is genuinely in the wording rather than in the biology. Darwin did not coin it; Spencer did, and Darwin adopted it in a later edition against his own better judgement. The problem is that 'fittest' in ordinary English suggests strength or athleticism, whereas in the technical sense it means nothing more than leaving more descendants. An organism that is smaller, slower and more timid than its rivals is fitter if it produces more surviving offspring, and often does. The circularity people complain about, that the fittest survive and we identify them by their survival, is real but harmless, because fitness is measured against specific traits in a specific environment rather than declared after the fact. Still, the phrase has done a century of damage, largely by lending biological vocabulary to social arguments that had nothing to do with biology.
options: The phrase was Spencer's rather than Darwin's, and it misleads because 'fittest' suggests strength while it technically means leaving more descendants, which has allowed the vocabulary to be misapplied to social arguments.
Darwin coined the phrase early in his career and defended it consistently, arguing that physical strength is the primary determinant of evolutionary success.
The speaker argues that the concept of fitness is entirely circular and should therefore be abandoned by working biologists.
The phrase accurately describes natural selection, and objections to it come from people who misunderstand basic evolutionary theory.

listening.transcript: One thing about presentations that I want to say before you start preparing. The most common mistake is not nervousness and it is not bad slides. It is running out of time and losing the conclusion. Almost every weak presentation I see has a strong middle and no ending, because the speaker has budgeted the time evenly across their material and then discovered at minute nine that there are four slides left. The fix is unglamorous. Decide what your last sentence is before you write anything else, rehearse the final two minutes more than any other part, and cut from the middle rather than from the end when you overrun. An argument without its conclusion is not a shortened argument; it is a different and much weaker one.
listening.q: What does the speaker identify as the main problem in weak presentations?
options: Speakers overrun and lose the conclusion because time is budgeted evenly.
Speakers are too nervous to deliver their material effectively.
Slides contain too much text and distract the audience.
Speakers rehearse the opening far more than the rest of the talk.

listening.spoken: Rice paddies are flooded not because rice requires standing water to grow but because most weeds cannot tolerate it. The crop will grow perfectly well in a drained field, and yields are sometimes higher but the labour of weeding rises sharply Flooding is therefore a herbicide rather than an irrigation method, which is why the practice persists even where water is expensive

The Sahara has not always been a desert Between roughly eleven and five thousand years ago it supported lakes, grassland and large populations of grazing animals, and rock paintings across the region show cattle, swimmers and hippopotamus. The change was driven by a slow shift in the tilt of the earth, which weakened the monsoon that had previously carried rain far to the north The transition took several centuries rather than happening abruptly.
